name: Atomic kernel
short: An atom's inner core, excluding its outer electrons.
body: Lewis's 1916 account distinguishes an inner kernel from an outer electron shell. In this terminology, the kernel comprises the nucleus and inner electrons; valence electrons lie outside it.
example: For carbon in a simple shell picture, the nucleus and two inner electrons form a core with net charge +4; four valence electrons sit outside.
note: This is historical chemical language. Kernel is not the usual modern name for an atomic nucleus, and Lewis's original atom model is not modern quantum mechanics.

sources.title: The Atom and the Molecule (1916)
sources.publisher: G. N. Lewis; JACS (historical paper transcription)

name: Flame / ignition kernel
short: A small ignition region that may grow into a flame.
body: A localized heated or reacting region initiates combustion. A successful ignition kernel develops into a self-sustaining flame; a weak one can be extinguished by heat loss or stretching.
example: A spark in an engine creates a small hot region. Whether that region survives and grows helps determine whether ignition succeeds.
note: Here kernel is a physical region, not a numerical filter used to simulate combustion.

sources.title: Analysis on ignition kernel formation in a quiescent mixture

name: Grain kernel
short: The grain itself, including its seed tissues.
body: In cereals, a kernel is a grain: botanically a caryopsis, a fruit whose wall is closely joined to the seed coat. A corn kernel contains protective outer tissues, endosperm and an embryo (germ).
example: A maize kernel contains a developing plant and stored food. Milling separates useful fractions such as germ, starch and fiber.
note: A corn kernel is not just the germ. Likewise, an acorn is a whole nut; its inner seed can be called its kernel.

name: Nuclear fuel kernel
short: The fuel-bearing core of a coated particle.
body: A TRISO particle encloses a small fuel kernel, commonly uranium dioxide or uranium oxycarbide, within protective carbon and silicon-carbide layers.
example: In a coated fuel particle, fission occurs in the fuel-bearing core; the surrounding layers retain fission products and protect the core.
note: This is a material component. A radiation point kernel is instead a mathematical response function.

name: Nut kernel
short: The seed or edible inner part inside a shell.
body: In nut processing, kernel names the inner seed material recovered when the shell is removed. Everyday culinary categories need not match botanical categories.
example: Crack a walnut: the lobed seed inside is the walnut kernel. Kernel color, shriveling and recovery yield are quality measurements.
note: An almond is botanically the seed of a drupe; the culinary label nut does not change what processors mean by kernel.

name: SPICE data kernel
short: A data file read by NASA's SPICE toolkit.
body: SPICE calls its mission-geometry and supporting-data files kernels. They can be binary or text and must be loaded before computations that need their contents.
example: Load ephemeris and time-conversion data, then ask SPICE for a body's position at a specified epoch. These kernels contain data; they are not launched as code.
note: SPICE here means the spacecraft toolkit, not the electronic-circuit simulator. A meta-kernel lists other kernels to load.
variants: Time-varying orientation / pointing; optional angular rates
